title: Multiplayer Camera Kit
user: Developers of small browser 2D co-op games who need a safe, inspectable camera that keeps several players visible without rebuilding framing math.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks which frameworks people use to create multiplayer 2D browser games, beyond PhaserJS.
A local-multiplayer developer calls multi-target camera scripting a massive hurdle and requests automatic bounding-box framing and zoom.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 game-development requests: choosing a browser multiplayer stack and avoiding heavy camera calculations for multi-character play.
current_workaround: Copy a camera gist, hand-code bounds and smoothing, hard-code split-screen thresholds, and tune it only after players fall off-screen.
incumbents_and_gap: Phaser, PixiJS, and Godot expose cameras but leave product-specific multi-target policies to each game. Existing snippets rarely provide a visible safety envelope or deterministic replay tests.
smallest_useful_product: An npm package for Canvas/WebGL games that takes player rectangles and world bounds, outputs camera position/zoom plus a debug overlay and deterministic trace runner. Non-goals: networking, rendering engine, split-screen renderer, or physics.
success_measure: A sample Phaser/Pixi game reaches stable two-to-four-player framing in under 30 lines of integration, and a supplied replay catches a deliberate off-screen regression.
monetization: free — engine-agnostic primitives benefit from open adoption; paid support is optional later.
constraints: Document coordinate and aspect-ratio assumptions; no player telemetry; preserve deterministic behaviour across frame rates; provide accessibility-safe zoom limits.
why_distinct: It is a narrowly scoped, testable multi-target camera policy rather than another game framework.
